Benign reactive cervical lymphadenopathy (reactive lymph node hyperplasia).

[THOUGHT] Analysis:
- The patient is a 40-year-old with a 3 x 3 cm anterior-triangle neck mass that has been progressively enlarging for ~3 weeks and was initially painless. Exam: non-tender, non-fluctuant, non-pulsatile. Ultrasound reported “normal” echotexture/vascularity/suspicious features but did not clarify whether the mass is intrathyroidal vs separate, or specific nodal features (hilum, cortical thickness, calcifications, matting). Ultrasound-guided FNA, cell block/IHC, and flow cytometry were reported as “normal,” but no detail on specimen adequacy or exact cytology wording (e.g., “benign/reactive lymphoid tissue” vs “non-diagnostic/insufficient”). Basic labs and vitals are unremarkable.

- Red flags present: age ≥40, a relatively large node (3 cm), progressive enlargement over weeks, and a painless node in the anterior triangle. These increase pre-test probability of malignancy (metastasis from head & neck SCC or other primaries, or lymphoma). A “normal” FNA + flow cytometry lowers but does not exclude malignancy — FNA sensitivity depends on sampling adequacy and the tumor type (metastatic carcinoma can sometimes be missed if sampling error occurs; some malignancies require tissue for architecture). Ultrasound report lacks key nodal descriptors. No ENT/oral cavity/nasopharyngeal exam findings provided. No smoking/sexual/HPV/HIV/TB risk history provided.

- Therefore the provided data are insufficient to conclusively call this benign reactive lymphadenopathy.

Red-flag/critical missing tests or information:
- Documentation of FNA adequacy and the full cytology/cell-block pathology report (exact wording, presence/absence of atypical/diagnostic cells).
- Whether the mass is truly a lymph node vs other entities (branchial cleft cyst, lipoma, thyroglossal duct cyst, intrathyroidal nodule) — ultrasound description of origin and nodal architecture (hilum, cortical thickness, calcifications, cystic change) is missing.
- Focused head & neck examination findings (oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx, larynx) and whether the mass is fixed vs mobile, relation to swallowing, overlying skin changes.
- Risk factors for head & neck malignancy (smoking, alcohol, sexual/HPV exposure), TB exposure, immunosuppression/HIV status.
- Consideration of cross-sectional imaging (CT neck with contrast) to evaluate nodal and regional anatomy.
- If concern persists or FNA was non-diagnostic: recommendation for excisional biopsy (preferred for definitive diagnosis) or core biopsy, and cultures/PCR for mycobacteria if suspected.

ANALYSIS: Silent (painless) thyroiditis is an inflammatory thyroid disorder causing transient thyrotoxicosis and thyroid dysfunction, whereas benign reactive cervical lymphadenopathy is enlargement of lymph nodes due to local/systemic immune stimulation—distinct anatomic sites, pathophysiology, clinical features, and management. Not equivalent.
